items.title: Managing Public Money and the accounting officer
items.body: Managing Public Money is HM Treasury's guide to handling public funds. It rests on four tests for any spending decision. Regularity means the spend is within the law and within the authority given. Propriety means it meets the standards of conduct Parliament and the public expect: honesty, openness and fair dealing. Value for money means getting the best outcome for the resources used. Feasibility means it can actually be delivered. The accounting officer of a department is personally accountable to Parliament for these. If a minister wants to go ahead with a spend the accounting officer thinks fails one of the tests, the accounting officer asks for a written ministerial direction, which is sent to the Comptroller and Auditor General and can be examined by the Public Accounts Committee.

questions.prompt: Which Treasury publication sets out the main rules for handling public funds?
Which list gives the four tests an accounting officer applies to spending?

options.text: Regularity, propriety, value for money, feasibility

questions.prompt: What does propriety mean in public spending?

options.text: That the spend is within the budget line
That the supplier offers the lowest price
Meeting the standards of conduct expected of public money, including honesty and openness
That the spend was approved by a committee

questions.prompt: A minister instructs you, as accounting officer, to go ahead with a spend you believe is poor value for money. What can you do and what happens next?
questions.answer: Set out the concerns in writing and ask for a written ministerial direction. If the direction is given, the accounting officer follows it, the direction is sent to the Comptroller and Auditor General, and the Public Accounts Committee may examine it. The advice and the direction are kept on record.
questions.rubric: Must say: put concerns in writing, request a written direction, follow it once given, direction goes to the C&AG and can be examined by the PAC/Parliament. Credit for noting the record is kept.

items.title: Budgets, forecasts and spending controls
items.body: A budget is the approved plan for income and spending. A forecast is the latest view of where spending will end up by the end of the year. Comparing them every month shows early whether a team will overspend or underspend. Moving money from one budget line to another is a virement and is allowed only within the rules and limits of the delegation. Spending controls, such as approval thresholds and sign-off from finance or a central team, exist so that large commitments are challenged before they are made. Nobody should commit money, for instance by signing a contract or placing an order, unless they hold the delegated authority to do so.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a budget and a forecast?

options.text: A budget is a prediction; a forecast is the approved plan
They are the same document at different dates
A budget covers income only; a forecast covers spending only
A budget is the approved plan; a forecast is the latest view of where spending will end up
Moving budget from one line to another within the rules

questions.prompt: Why do spending controls set approval thresholds?

options.text: So larger commitments are challenged and authorised before the money is committed
To guarantee that the cheapest option is chosen

questions.prompt: Four months into the year, your monthly report forecasts a 12% overspend. What do you do?
questions.answer: Check the forecast is accurate and find the cause. Work out options to reduce spend, re-plan timing or seek funds, agree them with finance, and escalate under the delegation if the overspend cannot be managed. Do not make new commitments without authority. Record decisions and report clearly to the board.
questions.rubric: Should verify the forecast, find causes, develop options with finance, escalate within delegated limits, avoid new commitments, and keep an audit trail and report to the board.

items.title: Paying suppliers and financial controls
items.body: Good financial control makes errors and fraud hard. A purchase order records what was agreed before anything is bought. When goods or services arrive they are checked and receipted. The supplier's invoice is then matched to the order and the receipt (a three-way match) before payment is made. The person who raises an order should not be the person who approves the payment, which is segregation of duties. Public bodies are expected to pay valid, undisputed invoices within 30 days, and sooner where policy says so, because late payment harms small suppliers. If an invoice looks wrong, it is queried in writing within the contract's terms rather than ignored or paid without checking.

questions.prompt: Within what time should valid, undisputed invoices normally be paid by a public body?

options.text: Having three people approve a budget
Matching the purchase order, the goods or services receipt and the invoice before paying

questions.prompt: Why should the person who raises a purchase order not also approve the payment?

options.text: Splitting the duties makes mistakes and fraud harder to carry out unnoticed
Because the approver should be a manager

questions.prompt: A supplier sends a large invoice for work nobody remembers ordering. There is no purchase order and they are chasing payment. What do you do?
questions.answer: Do not pay until it is verified. Check for a contract or authority, ask the budget holders and the supplier for evidence of the order and the delivery, and treat it as a possible fraud or control failure if it cannot be explained. Dispute it in writing within the terms, report the control gap, and fix the process so there is no spend without an order.
questions.rubric: Should refuse to pay without verification, investigate authority and delivery, consider fraud and report, respond in writing within terms, and fix the control gap (no PO, no pay).

items.title: Annual accounts and local government finance
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money; Local Government Finance Act 1988
items.body: Public bodies publish annual accounts that show income, spending, assets and liabilities for the year, so the public can see how money was used. An independent external auditor examines the accounts and gives an opinion on whether they are properly prepared and give a true and fair view. A clean opinion is unqualified; a qualified opinion means a material problem or limit was found. In English councils the statutory chief finance officer is the Section 151 officer, who must make sure the finances are sound. If a council cannot balance its budget, the Section 151 officer issues a Section 114 notice, which stops new spending apart from essential commitments while members decide what to do.

questions.prompt: What do a public body's annual accounts show?

options.text: Its income, spending, assets and liabilities for the year
Only the spending of the chief executive
Only the budget for next year

questions.prompt: Who is the statutory chief finance officer of an English council?
When is a Section 114 notice issued?

options.text: When the council wins a grant
When the council's spending will exceed the money it has available

questions.prompt: What does an external audit opinion tell readers, and what does a qualified opinion mean?
questions.answer: It is an independent view on whether the accounts are properly prepared and give a true and fair view. An unqualified opinion is clean. A qualified opinion means the auditor found a material misstatement or could not get enough evidence, and the body must explain and fix it. The auditor also reports on value-for-money arrangements to the audit committee.
questions.rubric: Should say independent opinion on true and fair view / proper preparation; unqualified = clean; qualified = material misstatement or limitation. Credit for audit committee reporting and value-for-money arrangements.
